title: The operator modulus |A|
subtitle: G2 lecture 035000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded companion deck developed from the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix. Adds explicit mathematical formulas, worked examples, and topic-specific diagrams while remaining standalone.

slides.title: Measuring output length without output direction
slides.lead: For a general linear map A, the modulus |A| captures how large the outputs are while forgetting where they point.
body: The map A may not be self-adjoint, so it need not admit a spectral theorem of the same form. But A* A is always positive, and therefore it has a unique positive square root.
That square root is called the modulus of A. It is the positive operator that will feed both singular-value theory and polar decomposition.
slides.takeaway: The modulus extracts the stretching behavior of A from the positive Gram operator A* A.

slides.title: Definition of the modulus
slides.lead: The modulus is defined by taking the positive square root of the Gram operator.
body: Because A* A is positive, the previous lecture guarantees that this definition makes sense and determines a unique positive operator on the source space of A.
The modulus lives on the input side. Even when A maps E to F with E and F different spaces, |A| is an operator on E.
slides.takeaway: |A| is always positive and always acts on the domain of A.

slides.title: Why it preserves output lengths
slides.lead: The squared norm of |A|x equals the squared norm of Ax for every input vector x.
body: This identity says that |A| records exactly the same output lengths as A, but does so through a positive self-adjoint operator on the input space. All directional information has been converted into an intrinsic stretching operator.
As a consequence, |A| and A have the same operator norm and the same singular values.
slides.takeaway: The modulus is the positive operator with exactly the same length profile as A.

slides.title: A two-dimensional example
slides.lead: Take A(x,y) = (2y,0). Then A* A is diagonal and the modulus is easy to compute.
body: The map ignores the first coordinate and doubles the second. The modulus does exactly the same amount of stretching, but keeps everything inside the original input space: it kills the horizontal direction and doubles the vertical direction.
Later the polar factor will restore the missing information that the doubled vertical direction is sent onto the horizontal output axis.
slides.takeaway: The modulus keeps the amount of stretching but not the final output direction.

slides.title: Three sanity checks
slides.lead: The definition agrees with familiar cases.
body: If A is already positive, then A* A = A² and the positive square root gives |A| = A. If A is unitary or orthogonal, then A* A = I, so |A| = I because such maps preserve lengths exactly. If A is diagonal with entries d_i, then |A| is diagonal with entries |d_i|.
These examples justify the name “modulus” by matching the scalar absolute-value picture.
slides.takeaway: The operator modulus generalizes ordinary absolute value and the notion of pure stretching.

slides.title: Kernel information survives
slides.lead: A vector is killed by A exactly when it is killed by |A|.
body: If Ax = 0, then the norm identity gives |||A|x|| = 0, so |A|x = 0. Conversely, if |A|x = 0, then ||Ax|| = 0 and therefore Ax = 0.
So the modulus forgets output direction, but it does not forget which input directions vanish completely.
slides.takeaway: The disappearing directions of A are encoded perfectly in the modulus.

slides.title: The norm of A is the top eigenvalue of |A|
slides.lead: Because |A| is positive, its spectral theory turns operator norms into eigenvalue statements.
body: The eigenvalues of |A| are the singular values of A. The largest singular value is the operator norm, and the full list of singular values describes how strongly A stretches in optimally chosen orthogonal directions.
Thus the modulus is the bridge from arbitrary linear maps to a positive operator whose spectrum measures stretching.
slides.takeaway: Singular values are simply the spectral values of the modulus.

slides.title: What the modulus forgets
slides.lead: Two different operators can have the same modulus if they stretch by the same amounts but send directions to different places.
body: A pure rotation and the identity both satisfy A* A = I, so both have modulus I. The modulus therefore does not encode where surviving vectors land; it only encodes how much length each input direction carries into the output.
Recovering that missing directional information is exactly the job of the polar factor in the next lecture.
slides.takeaway: The modulus measures stretching, not orientation or output placement.

slides.title: Why |A| is the right precursor to polar decomposition
slides.lead: Once the stretching part is isolated, what remains should preserve lengths on the surviving directions.
body: The identity ||Ax|| = |||A|x|| suggests that A should factor as a length-preserving map composed after |A|. That is the idea of polar decomposition: write A = U|A|, where U is a partial isometry.
The modulus therefore provides the positive part of the decomposition, while the polar factor carries the geometric direction data.
slides.takeaway: The modulus is the positive half of polar decomposition.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.lead: The modulus repackages a general linear map into a positive stretching operator.
body: Define |A| as the positive square root of A* A. Then |A| preserves the output lengths of A, has the same kernel as A, and has singular values equal to its eigenvalues. It lives on the input space and forgets only the final output direction.
That is exactly the information we need before building the polar factor.
slides.takeaway: |A| is the canonical positive record of how A stretches vectors.
